children: By Hannah Erin Lang
Alex Comez is still a bit wary of the whole artificial intelligence thing. But when shares of Anthropic start trading later this month, he wants in.

Comez, a 29-year-old chemist in Fargo, N.D., knows AI will probably upend the global economy. He suspects it might even come for his job one day. A few weeks ago, he drove past a data center in Iowa and found the sight unnerving: a "strange, eerie" place, he said, that produced a constant humming sound.

He's still joining the crowd waiting in line for what is expected to be one of the biggest initial public offerings ever. It is a necessary step, Comez said, to avoid being left behind as AI sets the pace for the stock market in the coming years.

"I don't really have a stake in the game unless I invest in it," said Comez, who also bought a few thousand dollars worth of SpaceX shares when that company went public earlier this year. "Buying into these institutions feels almost like the last chopper out of Saigon."

The mixed emotions Comez and other individual investors feel about Anthropic and AI stands in stark relief to the euphoria that greeted the IPO of Elon Musk's SpaceX five months ago. AI fever was at its peak, powering a blistering chip-stock rally that tripled or even quadrupled stocks including Sandisk and Intel. The S&P 500 had just logged one of its best two-month stretches in history. And there was the star power of Musk himself. Few would confuse Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's following or social-media output with the SpaceX chief's.

Anthropic will step into the public markets next week under markedly different circumstances. A decisive Democratic sweep in the midterm elections is sending a wave of AI-skeptic politicians into state and federal offices across the country. Wall Street is reeling from the still-fresh departure of Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia and arguably the tech sector's North Star. And many Americans, like Comez, are starting to grapple with the consequences of the stock market's massive, singular bet on AI technology.

The question is whether Anthropic's $1.3 trillion offering can revive the excitement around AI that has sputtered in recent weeks. And if the IPO doesn't come close to SpaceX's record-breaking offering in winning over retail, it is a sign the bloom may be off Wall Street's favorite bet.

"People are questioning AI in general," said Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at the investment-research firm Vanda, which tracks retail trading flows. "They're just not buying as aggressively as they have been. An Anthropic IPO last summer would have been very different."
Falling Out of Love
As this summer began, Tim McLean started thinking he might have sold too early.

The 60-year-old debt broker had already unloaded his Micron shares for a 30% return back in February, when the stock was trading around $420 a share — not bad, he remembered thinking at the time. But then he watched from his home office in Naples, Fla., as the price climbed past $500. Then $700. Then $1,000.
"I felt a little bit lonely," McLean said. "I was definitely left out"

By June, the AI investment boom that powered stock returns had reached a fever pitch. A frenzy for memory chips more than doubled semiconductor stocks such as Micron and Advanced Micro Devices, with some names notching double-digit gains in a single day. Analysts lifted their year-end forecasts as the gains accelerated. When the chipmaker Cerebras went public in May, shares rose nearly 70% in the first day of trading.

Then, SpaceX went public. The enthusiasm, especially from everyday investors, helped the rocket maker pull off a goldilocks debut. Individual traders alone requested $100 billion worth of shares and flocked to the Robinhood app in such large numbers that the brokerage reported outages.
Wall Street took the success of SpaceX as a good omen for other offerings this year. But as the summer progressed, the red-hot tech rally began to cool.

Escalating costs of the AI build-out drew more scrutiny from stock analysts. A bond selloff and a rate increase from the Federal Reserve lifted borrowing costs as hyperscalers such as Meta and Amazon sought to raise hundreds of billions of dollars to finance their AI efforts. Investors' wait for AI companies to turn their spending spree into profits took on more urgency.

As the markets' challenges mounted, individual investors dialed back their stock-buying. From the beginning of May through the end of September, net retail turnover declined some 40%, Vanda's data show. These traders — who once plowed into equities so aggressively they helped pull the market out of its "Liberation Day" tariffs selloff — were growing more cautious and selective.

"I don't think retail is falling out of love with AI," said Gav Blaxberg, a 28-year-old investor who runs a financial media company geared toward young retail investors. "I just think they're falling out of love with paying any price for it."

Americans have also grown more anxious about the risks posed by AI. Those fears were amplified by reports of rogue AI agents wreaking havoc, as well as remarks from Amodei and competitor Sam Altman backing an industrywide slowdown on AI model development. In one WSJ poll, 63% of voters said they wanted to see a pause in both AI development and the data-center build-out.

The midterm election crystallized the backlash. Americans voted overwhelmingly for data-center moratoriums and AI-wary candidates. The concern that those results would slow the breakneck AI build-out helped send stocks to their worst day since the tariff turmoil in more than a year, with the Nasdaq notching a 5.5% drop on the day.

The volatility further dampened investors' appetite. In the days leading up to the midterms, retail purchases dropped to among their lowest levels of the year, according to JPMorgan Chase. Vanda's data showed that last Thursday's selloff marked the biggest day of single-stock selling among individual investors since the Covid crash of March 2020.
And investors like McLean, who sold all of his tech stocks as the volatility unfolded, aren't eager to dive back into the fray soon. He'll be sitting out the Anthropic IPO.
"I'm 60. I can't take a 50% drawdown in my portfolio," he said of the AI trade. "When one of your risk profiles is that you can kill humanity, that doesn't make me want to jump and buy the stock."
'Game-changers'
Others see an opportunity to hitch their wagon to a company forging the AI frontier. Stephen Cruise, a 64-year-old retiree near Detroit, has requested shares of Anthropic at the listing price.

Cruise said he uses Anthropic's Claude often to set budgets, plan vacations and research potential investments. He also thinks AI is going to totally transform society — in a good way, Cruise specified — and wants a piece of the companies making it happen.

"These companies are game-changers," said Cruise, who also bought shares of SpaceX when it debuted. "I just want to be a part of the growth opportunity." He has been strategically taking profits in other stocks such as Apple and Eli Lilly to have some cash ready to buy Anthropic.

Analysts were quick to note that a recent cool-down in retail buying doesn't mean that individual investors are disappearing from the market — and many still expect there to be significant demand for shares of Anthropic, even if it doesn't quite reach the frenetic heights of SpaceX. Anthropic is expected to allocate up to 20% of its IPO shares to individual investors, which would be a higher-than-average figure.

And there were some aspects of the SpaceX debut that were always going to be challenging for any company to replicate — specifically, the allure of Musk, who maintains a kind of cult status among individual investors that stretches back years.

A successful Anthropic IPO could end up giving the AI trade the boost it needs to regain momentum. The company's new targeted valuation of $1.3 trillion, well below initial estimates as high as $2 trillion, could lure more retail buyers off the fence.

Many individual investors have shown a willingness to take a chance on tech stocks, especially as the yearslong bull market has kept rolling forward. The cost of missing out on the next move higher, some said, is still too great.
"There's a risk of a bubble, for sure," Cruise said. "I recognize that.
"There's money to be made in the meantime."
